transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Stocks rebounded this morning after last week's big selloff.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones industrial average jumped more than 700 points
in early trading.
Crude oil prices are falling with the U.S. benchmark dropping below $90 a barrel.
AAA says retail gasoline prices have fallen to just over $4 a gallon.
That's down about $0.37 from a month ago, although gas still cost over a dollar a gallon
more than when the U.S. launched its war with Iran.
Diesel prices have also fallen by about a dime a gallon over the last month.
Stocking Nvidia is down this morning after the chipmaker's board announced an investigation
into reports the company's CEO was the target of a foreign spy effort.
CEO Jensen Wong reportedly had an affair with a business customer who is suspected of working
for the Chinese government.
China's foreign ministry denies that.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
President Trump is hosting Qatar's prime minister at the White House today.
There to discuss the latest Iranian offer to end the current stalemate.
But as NPR's Aya Batrawi reports, the two sides remain far apart on key issues.
Qatar has been leading mediation efforts between Tehran and Washington to try and get the two
sides to agree on a temporary ceasefire that would lead to direct talks again.
But Secretary of State Marco Rubio says Washington and Tehran are not yet on the verge of a breakthrough.
He told reporters over the weekend that Iran's demands are, in his words, outrageous and
ridiculous and not really realistic.
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman responded to that in a briefing into Tehran, saying
it's not ridiculous to demand that the U.S. lift sanctions and its naval blockade on Iranian
ships as a prerequisite for direct talks.
Iran's government has been gloating in posts online and in official comments following
the Democrats' midterm sweep, saying it proves how unpopular this war is.
Aya Batrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Esenkot,
to try to form the next Israeli government.
NPR's Lorne Freya reports from Tel Aviv today is Esenkot's first full day of coalition-building
efforts.
Center-right Gadi Esenkot won slightly fewer votes in last month's Israeli election than
his rival, incumbent Prime Minister Netanyahu, on the far right.
But neither won a majority, and more of the other political parties want Esenkot to govern.
In a ceremony at the president's office, Esenkot said his door is open to coalition
partners.
But that anyone who tries to thwart coalition-building for personal reasons will, quote, "be remembered
in history as someone who failed to save Israel."
That's a reference to any moves by Netanyahu who has alleged election fraud without evidence,
and remains caretaker Prime Minister during this process.
Lauren Freya, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
On Wall Street, the Dow is now up more than 800 points.
You're listening to NPR.
British actor and comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced by a British court to more
than 10 years in prison.
This is for his convictions last week on rape and sexual assault charges.
British police say they are now investigating further rape allegations against Brand from
two other women.
In the U.S., homelessness saw a major drop last year, the largest in more than a decade.
NPR's Jennifer Ludden reports it was down for the second year in a row.
The federal housing agency HUD announced the decline of more than 6 percent, and it touted
Trump administration policies, like closing the southern border, as a key factor.
Several cities with big drops had seen an earlier surge of asylum seekers in homeless
shelters.
A separate analysis, commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness, also finds a
broad decline, says the group's CEO, Ann Oliva.
It's good news that more people are getting housed and that the programs that are funded
by Congress are working.
The Trump administration has tried to overhaul those programs but has so far been blocked
by courts.
Despite the latest decline, nearly 700,000 people remain without housing.
Jennifer Ludden in Pierre News, Washington.
One of the world's remaining religious shakers has died.
The Sabbath Day Lake Shaker Village of Maine says Sister June Carpenter died last week.
She was 88 years old.
The Sabbath Day community dates back to 1783.
It is the last one in the world and has a handful of shaker members.
I'm Corbett Coleman, NPR News, in Washington.
This message comes from Rince.
Your dog believes you are magnificent.
Capable of anything.
Your dog has watched you spend hours a week moving fabric between machines and has never
once lost faith.
The question was never whether you could become the person your dog thinks you are.
It's what's in the way.
It turns out, just a laundry.
Not anymore.
Rince picks up your laundry, cleans it expertly, and delivers it back while you get on with
being magnificent.
Sign up today at rinse.com.
Rince, it's time to be great.

topics.text: Stocks rebound as Dow jumps more than 700 points after last week's selloff
Gas prices fall to just over $4 a gallon, though still above pre-Iran-war levels
Nvidia shares drop after board probes reports CEO Jensen Huang was target of foreign spy effort
Qatar's prime minister visits White House to discuss Iran's ceasefire offer
Rubio calls Iran's demands outrageous as Tehran says lifting sanctions is reasonable
Israeli President taps Gadi Eisenkot to form next government, rival to Netanyahu
Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years in prison for rape and sexual assault
U.S. homelessness drops more than 6 percent in 2025, largest decline in over a decade
Sister June Carpenter, one of the last Shakers, dies at age 88 in Maine
